analysis.one_liner: Orders the Treasury Secretary to break up the nation's largest banks within one year.
analysis.headline: Senator Sanders' bill to break up the biggest Wall Street banks never got a single cosponsor and died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Financial Stability Oversight Council to list every bank whose failure would require a taxpayer bailout, then require the Treasury Secretary to break those banks up within a year. It would also cut listed banks off from Federal Reserve emergency lending and stop them from using federally insured deposits to fund speculative derivatives trading. Its goal is to end the 'too big to fail' problem, where the biggest banks know taxpayers will rescue them if they collapse, as happened in 2008.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and bank customers, who would no longer be on the hook to rescue enormous banks, and whose insured savings would be shielded from risky trading. Smaller banks and credit unions would also gain if their biggest competitors were broken apart.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Financial Stability Oversight Council to compile a list of 'Too Big To Fail' entities, including the U.S. banks the international Financial Stability Board has identified as systemically important, and submit it to Congress and the President [S2] [S3].

Requires the Treasury Secretary, within one year, to break up every entity on that list so that its failure would no longer cause a catastrophic effect on the U.S. or global economy without a taxpayer bailout [S2] [S3].

Prohibits listed entities from accessing any Federal Reserve credit facility or the discount window — the emergency lending that was central to the 2008 rescues — including asset purchases, bridge loans, and capital injections [S2] [S3].

Bars listed banks and their owners from using federally insured deposits to fund hedging, speculative derivatives, or derivatives dealing, and from conducting those activities in ways that put insured deposits or the Deposit Insurance Fund at risk [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The handful of giant bank holding companies identified as systemically important — roughly a dozen firms including JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley — which would be broken into smaller pieces and lose their implicit taxpayer guarantee. Shareholders and executives of those firms would bear much of the cost, and defenders of the banks argue breaking them up could reduce economies of scale and complicate banking services for some large customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: The largest Wall Street bank holding companies

drawbacks.text: The bill hands the Treasury Secretary enormous one-year discretion to break up private companies with no detailed process, standards, or judicial review beyond consulting each firm's regulator — critics would call that excessive, vaguely bounded executive power over private business [S3].

The mandate is arguably unworkable as written: it gives the Secretary one year to dismantle institutions with trillions in assets and worldwide operations, and the actual mechanics of divestiture are left entirely open [S3].

Denying Federal Reserve emergency lending even as a backstop could, in a true crisis, leave the financial system with fewer tools to stop contagion, a cost an honest supporter must weigh against ending bailouts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: in 2008 the largest banks were rescued with taxpayer money and emergency Fed lending precisely because they were too big to let fail, and that implicit guarantee lets them borrow more cheaply than smaller competitors. This bill attacks that directly. Its serious weakness is execution: it delegates the entire breakup to the Treasury Secretary in one year with little process, which courts and Congress would have fought over, and cutting all Fed emergency access is blunter than needed. On balance, the direction is sound and the design is crude.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced by Senator Sanders with zero cosponsors, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day of introduction, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on May 6, 2015, during his presidential campaign, framing it as an answer to the 2008 bailouts [S1] [S3].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor — zero in total — over the entire two-year Congress [S4].
The Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, chaired by Senator Richard Shelby, took no recorded action: no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest Wall Street banks kept their size, their access to the Federal Reserve backstop, and their ability to fund derivatives trading with insured deposits; no taxpayer money was saved and no bank was broken up.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it received no other Senate support; it was referred to the Banking Committee and went no further [S1] [S4] [S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Richard Shelby (R-AL)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Large bank holding companies identified as systemically important
against.role: The roughly dozen U.S. banks the bill would break up (e.g., JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs)
against.what_they_did: Would have been dismantled and stripped of Fed emergency lending and deposit-funded trading; the banking industry actively opposed breakup proposals of this kind during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator supported the bill and none opposed it in writing — there was no vote, so no party split is measurable; the Republican-chaired Banking Committee simply never acted on it [S5].

industries.industry: Large bank holding companies (systemically important U.S. banks)
industries.note: The bill would break these firms up within a year, cut them off from Federal Reserve emergency lending, and bar them from funding derivatives trading with insured deposits. Their interest in remaining intact is exactly what ordinary taxpayers pay for when one of them fails and must be rescued.

If the giants were broken up, smaller banks would face less competition from rivals whose 'too big to fail' status lets them borrow more cheaply. This is a competitive effect rather than a direct provision of the bill.
The bill would remove emergency lending tools the Fed used in 2008 and give the Treasury Secretary sweeping breakup authority, restructuring who holds crisis-management power.
